Florence, November. Pietro and Davide went together to the premiere of a film about the 1966 flood, shot right in via Maggio. Mancini has asked each of them for a review for the youth page of the "Gazzetta". Now he reads them both.
Pietro, yours begins like this: "The most beautiful film I've ever seen. Perfect. You absolutely must see it."
Why, isn't it good? I loved it.
It's not a review, it's applause. And yours, Davide: "Slow, predictable, didactic. Pietro's grandmother acts better than the actors."
But it's true! Graziella has only one line and it's the best scene.
Maybe. But a review is neither applause nor a demolition. It's a reasoned judgement. You need the strong points and the weak points.
Then I could say: "Although slow in places, the film is decidedly moving."
There. "A tratti" tones it down, "decisamente" strengthens it. And you, Davide, can say it's predictable, but "rather", not "completely".
"The screenplay is rather predictable, but the photography is anything but banal." Like that?
Perfect. And at the end the verdict, in one sentence. The reader must know whether to go to the cinema or not.
And what if we wrote a single review, the two of us? Him the criticism, me the praise.
Now that's an idea. It'll be called "For and against". You have two days.
Stress on "GEN": co-in-vol-GEN-te. The "o" and "i" are pronounced separately.
"Bello" and "brutto" say almost nothing in a review. Choose the adjective that explains WHY: "coinvolgente" says it keeps you hooked; "commovente" says it moves you.
"Tutt'altro che" = anything but. It negates forcefully, but elegantly:
"Il film è tutt'altro che noioso" = the film is NOT at all boring (in fact it's interesting). It's a litotes: you say the positive by denying the negative.

Concession is the heart of a balanced review: you acknowledge a flaw before praising, or a quality before criticising. The reader trusts you.

The film was called "The angels of the mud" and was the first feature film by Sofia Marchetti, a twenty-nine-year-old Florentine director who had won a small prize in Venice with a short film about the workshops of the Oltrarno. She had shot it the previous spring, over six weeks, almost entirely in via Maggio, because it was one of the few streets in the centre where, she said, "the façades haven't yet become a postcard". For a month and a half the street had been invaded by lorries, lights, cables, extras dressed as in 1966 and an enormous machine that sprayed fake mud, made of clay and water, onto the shop shutters. Guido the shoemaker had protested three times. Then the director had offered him a small part, that of a shoemaker, naturally, and he had stopped protesting.

Those six weeks were the strangest in the recent history of via Maggio. Every morning at six the production lorries blocked the street, and the fruit seller had to park her van two blocks away, which she commented on aloud in words that can't be written. Bellini was called in as a consultant for the restorers' scenes: he explained to the actors how paintings were washed in 1966, with sponges and clean water, and how Japanese paper was laid on panels to prevent the paint from falling off. Viola was an extra in a crowd scene, in a stranger's arms, and cried at the wrong moment. Lupino ruined a four-minute take by crossing the street with a loaf in his mouth. The director, instead of getting angry, kept the scene in the edit. "It's the only thing nobody acted," she said.

Graziella was in the film too. She didn't want to be, at first. She said she had lived through 1966 once, and once had been enough. But Sofia Marchetti had come to eat at the trattoria four evenings in a row, had listened to her stories, had read the chapter "The loaf" in Bellini's book, and on the fifth evening had asked her whether she would play herself as an old woman, in a scene at the end of the film. A single line. Graziella had said no three times, then yes, on one condition: that the ribollita in the scene be real, and hers. So, in the last scene of the film, an old lady in a white apron served a bowl of steaming ribollita to a young volunteer, looked him in the eye and said: "Eat. Mud doesn't come off on an empty stomach."

That scene, the director said later, took fourteen takes. Not because Graziella got it wrong, but because each time she said a different line. In the first take she said: "Eat, you're all mud." In the second: "Eat, the river won't wait." In the third she added a dialect word the sound engineer didn't understand. The screenwriter, a girl from Rome, was in despair. At the tenth take Sofia Marchetti stopped everything, sat down next to Graziella and asked her what she had really said, that November day in 1966, to the young Aldo covered in mud. Graziella thought for a long time. "I didn't say anything," she replied. "I was twelve. I gave him the bowl and ran into the kitchen." Then she added: "But my mother said something. She said mud doesn't come off on an empty stomach." The fourteenth take was the good one. It was her mother's line.

The premiere was on a Thursday evening in November, at the La Compagnia cinema, in via Cavour, a few days before the anniversary of the flood. The auditorium was full: there were the actors, the crew, the producers, the journalists, and a whole row of via Maggio residents who wanted to see their street on the big screen. Graziella sat in the third row, in her coat for great occasions, between Bellini and Efisio, who in the film was played by a twenty-five-year-old Sardinian actor who, in his opinion, looked nothing like him. Pietro and Davide sat behind them, each with a notebook. Mancini had asked both of them to write a review for the "Gazzetta"'s new youth page, which would be called "Under twenty". It was the first time anyone had paid Pietro to write: twenty euros a review.

The film lasted two hours and twenty minutes. It told the story of Marco, a boy from Bologna who in November 1966 comes to Florence by bicycle to help save the city, falls in love with the daughter of an Oltrarno trattoria owner and decides to stay. Pietro understood after five minutes that Marco was, largely, his grandfather Aldo, even though the director had changed his name "out of respect for the family". The bicycle was red, with a basket. The girl was twelve at the beginning of the film and eighteen at the end, when he comes back to look for her. There were scenes of mud in the streets, of students passing the books of the National Library from hand to hand, of restorers washing paintings with sponges. And there was a scene, about halfway through, in which an old restorer handed Marco a big brush with blue bristles. Bellini, in the third row, took off his glasses and wiped his eyes.

Efisio, on the other hand, spent the film correcting it under his breath. When on screen the students passed the books of the National Library along a long human chain, he murmured: "There were more of us. And it was raining." When the actor playing him lifted a crate of books on his own, he snorted: "It took four people." When a Sardinian volunteer, in the film, sang a folk song in the rain, Efisio stopped correcting and sat motionless. It was the song of his village. Nobody had asked him for it, nobody had interviewed him about that song. The director had found it, she explained later, in an old recording in the Rai archives, from December 1966, in which a group of Sardinian boys sang in the mud at Santa Croce. "That's me," Efisio whispered to Bellini. "Third from the left. You can hear I'm out of tune." Bellini squeezed his arm in the dark.

When the lights came up, there was long applause. The director went up on stage with the actors, thanked via Maggio, thanked "Signora Graziella, without whom this film wouldn't have an ending", and asked Graziella to come up on stage. Graziella refused, then stood up, then sat down again, then was literally lifted by Efisio and Bellini and escorted to the steps. On stage, in front of three hundred people, she took the microphone the director held out to her, looked at it as you look at an unfamiliar ladle and said a single sentence: "The film is beautiful. But my husband came on foot, not by bicycle. My father gave him the bicycle later." The auditorium burst out laughing. The director went red. "I knew," she said into the microphone. "But by bicycle it was more cinematic." Graziella gave her back the microphone. "Exactly," she said.

Walking home along the Arno, Pietro and Davide argued for half an hour. Pietro had adored the film. He said it was the most beautiful he had ever seen, that it had his grandfather, his grandmother, Bellini, the trattoria, the blue brush, everything. Davide said the film was slow, that it was at least half an hour too long, that the love story was predictable from the first minute and that the dialogue explained everything, as if the audience were stupid. "The only real scene is your grandmother's," he said. "A single line, and it's worth more than two hours of film." Pietro took offence. Davide took offence because Pietro had taken offence. They reached via Maggio without speaking, and that evening each wrote his review alone, shut in his room, like two enemies preparing a duel.

Pietro, that night, couldn't write. Every sentence seemed too little. So he did something he had never done: he looked up the reviews of famous critics online, those of the big national newspapers, to see how they wrote. He read about twenty. Some were so enthusiastic they looked like adverts. Others were so savage they looked like personal revenge. One, by a critic from Milan, demolished a film in ten lines without ever saying what it was about. Pietro went down to the kitchen, where Giulia was washing the dishes, and asked her how you judge something you like so much. Giulia thought about it, her hands in the water. "When I went on television against Ruggeri," she said, "I learned one thing. If you defend everything, nobody believes you. If you admit a flaw, they believe you about the rest too." Pietro went back to his room and reread his review. There wasn't a single flaw in it.

The next morning they took their reviews to Mancini, at the "Gazzetta" office, where the cat Titolo was asleep on the keyboard of a switched-off computer. Mancini read both, in silence, while the boys waited standing, without looking at each other. Pietro's was a page and a half long and full of adjectives: very beautiful, perfect, wonderful, unforgettable. It ended: "You absolutely must see it. Five stars out of five." Davide's was ten lines long and full of other adjectives: slow, predictable, didactic, rhetorical. It ended: "The only thing that saves the film is Pietro's grandmother. One star out of five, and the star is hers." Mancini put the sheets down on the table. "Neither of them is a review," he said. "Pietro's is applause. Davide's is a demolition. And neither of you has written why."

Then Mancini gave them a lesson that lasted all morning, between one phone call and the next. He explained that a review serves one purpose only: to help the reader decide whether it's worth spending two hours and ten euros to see a film. That's why it must be reasoned. "Very beautiful" means nothing. "Gripping" means you don't look at your watch. "Moving" means you cry. "Predictable" means you already know how it ends. Then he explained how to tone down and how to strengthen a judgement. "Rather slow" isn't the same as "decidedly slow". "Boring in places" isn't the same as "boring". And finally he explained the most important thing: concession. "Before you criticise, acknowledge a quality," he said. "Before you praise, acknowledge a flaw. Although slow, the film is moving. Although the photography is splendid, the story is predictable. If you do that, the reader trusts you."

It was Pietro who had the idea. He looked at Davide for the first time since the evening before and said: "What if we wrote a single review, the two of us? You the criticism, me the praise. And at the end a verdict together." Davide thought about it. Then he nodded, still a little offended. Mancini slapped the table, waking the cat. "Now that's an idea," he said. "One column on the left and one on the right. For and against. But with one rule: each of you must concede something to the other. Pietro must admit at least one flaw, and Davide at least one quality that isn't the grandmother." The two looked at each other. "You have two days," said Mancini. "And seven hundred characters each. Not one more." Pietro asked what "battute" were. "Characters, spaces included," replied Mancini. "In a newspaper space is more precious than talent."

Counting the characters turned out to be quite a business. Pietro would write a sentence, count it letter by letter, then rewrite it shorter and count it again. After three hours he discovered the computer could count them by itself, and felt stupid. Davide, who wrote by hand, didn't have that advantage: he counted with a pencil, making a little stroke every ten characters, as he had done with Bardi's connectors at the debate. When they met at the trattoria, on the afternoon of the second day, Viola offered to help them. She was five and could count to a hundred. She counted the first line of Davide's review three times, getting three different results, then declared that there were "too many" words and that some had to go. Davide looked at her, then at his sentence about the soundtrack, long and full of adjectives, and crossed it out. "She's right," he said. "It was too much."

Writing seven hundred characters was the hardest thing Pietro had ever done, harder than the labels and Researchers' Night. A page and a half of enthusiasm had to become five sentences. He had to choose. He removed "very beautiful", removed "perfect", removed "unforgettable". He kept "moving", because it was true: he had cried twice. He added "gripping", because that was true too: he hadn't looked at his watch once. And then, with great effort, he wrote the concession: "Although slow in places and far too long, the film manages to…". He stopped. Manages to what? He thought about it for an hour. Then he found the sentence. "…manages to make the viewer smell the mud and feel the warmth of the ribollita." He read it to Graziella, who was ironing in the kitchen. Graziella nodded without looking up. "The mud smelled worse," she said. "But it'll do."

Davide, at home in San Frediano, in his mother's kitchen, had the opposite problem. Ten lines of criticism had to become seven hundred balanced characters, with at least one quality that wasn't Graziella. He replayed the film in his head, scene by scene, as he did with paintings when he had to copy them. And he noticed something that, on the night of the premiere, his anger had prevented him from seeing: the photography. The mud scenes were shot in grey-green light, almost colourless, like the black-and-white photographs of 1966. Then, when Marco enters the trattoria for the first time, the light becomes warm, golden, like a seventeenth-century painting. "It's like Caravaggio," thought Davide. "Darkness outside, light inside." He wrote: "Although the screenplay is rather predictable, the photography is anything but banal: the mud is grey as fear, the trattoria golden as a refuge."

They wrote the final verdict together, on the evening of the second day, on the trattoria steps, with a notebook on their knees and a single pen, which they passed back and forth. They argued again, but this time over a single word. Pietro wanted to write "a must-see". Davide wanted to write "worth seeing, with patience". It took them half an hour. In the end they found a sentence neither of them entirely liked, which, said Davide, was probably the sign that it was right: "An imperfect and sincere film which, despite a few longueurs, deserves to be seen. Especially by those who think Florence is just a museum. Three and a half stars: three for the film, half for the ribollita." Pietro reread the sentence and laughed. "The half star for the ribollita is yours," he said. "I know," replied Davide. "It's the only concession that cost me nothing."

Mancini read the final version on Friday morning, at the office, red pencil in hand, while the two boys waited holding their breath. This time he read it twice. Then he took the pencil and changed a single word: in Pietro's column, "far too long" became "a little too long". "'Far too' is a judgement," he explained. "'A little too' is an observation. You're the one doing the 'for', Pietro. You must admit the flaw, but gracefully." Then he looked at Davide's column and changed nothing. "Your sentence about the mud being grey as fear," he told him, "will be stolen. You'll see. In a month you'll find it in some famous critic's review, without your name." Davide blushed. Mancini signed the sheet at the bottom, as he did with articles ready for print, and handed it to the layout designer. "Go home," he said. "On Sunday you're on the newsstands."

The review came out the following Sunday, on the front page of the "Under twenty" section, with a headline chosen by Mancini: "For and against: two fifteen-year-olds and a film about the flood". On the left Pietro's column, on the right Davide's, in the middle the joint verdict, and above a small drawing by Davide: two boys sitting at the cinema, one crying and one looking at his watch. The paper sold like hot cakes in via Maggio. The fruit seller bought five copies. Guido the shoemaker cut out the review and put it in his window, because in Davide's column it said that "the shoemaker, played by a real shoemaker, is more convincing than half the actors". Graziella said nothing. But that evening, on the kitchen shelf, next to Pietro's crooked cup and Viorica's photograph, the newspaper page appeared, carefully folded, with the sentence about the half star underlined in pencil.

Three days later a letter arrived at the office addressed "To the two reviewers of Under twenty". It was from Sofia Marchetti, the director. Mancini brought it to the trattoria and had Pietro read it aloud. The director wrote that she had read dozens of reviews of her film, some enthusiastic, some savage, almost all written by famous critics. "Yours is the only one that taught me something," she wrote. "Pietro is right: the film is moving. Davide is right: it's too long and the dialogue explains too much. I was about to start editing the television version. I'll cut twenty minutes. And I'll remove three lines that explain what the images already say." At the end she had added: "P.S. Tell Signora Graziella that in the television version Marco will arrive on foot. Her father will give him the bicycle later."

Mancini had been right about Davide's sentence too. Three weeks later, in a major national daily, the film's review appeared, signed by a very well-known critic, and halfway through the article it said: "The mud, in the film, is grey as fear." Davide read it at the newsstand and was speechless. Pietro wanted to write to the paper to protest. Mancini stopped them both. "No," he said. "It's the greatest compliment you could receive. It means the sentence was good. Good sentences travel on their own, and sometimes forget where they started from." Then he added, laughing: "And anyway I've got the date. Ours came out first. If one day that gentleman wants to be clever, I'll send him the page." Davide cut out both reviews and stuck them side by side in his sketchbook, with an arrow and a caption: "Set out from via Maggio."

Graziella, who had been listening from the kitchen, came out with floury hands and asked for the postscript to be read twice. Then she sat down at the boys' table, something she almost never did during service. "Do you want to know the truth?" she said. Pietro and Davide nodded. "When Aldo arrived, on the third day, he'd walked from Prato, covered in mud up to his waist. My father gave him food and a place to sleep in the cellar. After a week, when Aldo said he had to go back to Bologna, my father gave him the red bicycle, the one with the basket, so he wouldn't have to walk back. And Aldo said: 'Then I'll bring it back.' It took him nine years to bring it back." She was silent for a moment, looking at Aldo's photograph on the shelf. "In the film," she said at last, "the bicycle comes too early. In life it came at the right moment. Write that, next time."

Pietro wrote it that very evening, in the black notebook, word for word. Below it he stuck the "For and against" review and the director's letter. Then he wrote a reflection, because by now the black notebook had also become the place where he thought. "I've learned that a judgement without reasons is just an emotion. And that an emotion without concessions is just cheering from the stands. Davide and I were both right, and we were both wrong. The right review was halfway, like the star for the ribollita." He reread the sentence, then added at the bottom, in small letters: "P.S. The film is still the most beautiful I've ever seen. But you can't write that in a review. In a diary you can." In San Frediano, in Rita's kitchen, the light was still on. Davide, that evening, was drawing a red bicycle arriving, at last, at the right moment.
